clue.text: Variation in tolls to modify telephone usage?

parts.note: to modify something is to change it
using the telephone is ringing someone up

explanation.surface: A suggestion that call charges be altered to curb how people use the phone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tolls' looks like phone charges, but it means the sounding of bells: change ringing is the English art of ringing a set of bells in shifting orders.
explanation.definitionFit: Change ringing is bell-ringing in which the order of the bells is varied each round, so the tolls vary.

clue.text: Encourage timid person to accept new rate

indicators.note: to accept something is to take it in, so one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: a hen, like a chicken, is a word for a fearful, timid person

indicators.note: new signals the letters of rate made afresh in another order

explanation.surface: Bolstering a nervous person by having them agree to a fresh pay rate.
explanation.walkthrough: A hen, like 'chicken', is slang for a coward; 'new' signals the rearranging, and 'to accept' sets the result inside after its first two letters.
explanation.definitionFit: To hearten someone is to give them courage, which is what encouraging means.

clue.text: North introduces diamonds -subtle

indicators.note: one piece introduces the next by standing in front of it

parts.note: ice is slang for diamonds

explanation.surface: A bridge-table picture: the North player leads diamonds, a subtle play.
explanation.walkthrough: 'diamonds' looks like the card suit but is the slang ICE for gems.
explanation.definitionFit: A nice distinction is a fine, delicate one, so nice can mean subtle.

clue.text: Piece cut out of Sun, apparently?

definitions.text: Piece cut out of Sun, apparently?

parts.words: Piece cut out of Sun, apparently?
parts.note: during a solar blackout the Moon seems to take a bite or a whole disc out of the Sun, as if a piece were cut away

explanation.surface: A newspaper clipping removed from the Sun tabloid.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sun' looks like the British tabloid newspaper, with a cutting taken from it; it is the star, which seems to lose a piece when the Moon passes in front.
explanation.definitionFit: In a solar eclipse the Moon hides part or all of the Sun's disc, so a piece seems missing.

clue.text: Take time in messing around, meanwhile

indicators.note: messing around with letters means jumbling them into a new order

parts.note: R, from the Latin recipe, is the abbreviation for take on a prescription

explanation.surface: Advice to slow down while fooling about, in the meantime.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Take' is the R written at the head of a prescription, from Latin recipe; 'messing around' signals the shuffle of all three pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Interim works as an adverb meaning in the meantime, an older sense synonymous with meanwhile.

clue.text: Valley in Luxembourg

annotationWithheld.why: Clue held as 'Valley in Luxembourg (4)': only the definition 'Valley' fits GLEN, and nothing in 'Luxembourg' supplies the letters; wordplay appears cut short, and searches found no fuller print.

clue.text: New expression for massaging ego, only?

indicators.note: massaging works the letters of ego and only into a fresh shape

explanation.surface: Someone coining a phrase purely to flatter their own vanity.
explanation.walkthrough: 'massaging' rearranges EGO plus ONLY into the seven letters needed.
explanation.definitionFit: Neology is the coining of new words, or such a coinage itself, so it is a newly made expression.

clue.text: Willing to change lodging

definitions.meaning: describes an obliging person ready to adapt
giving someone a room, putting them up

explanation.definitionFit: An obliging person adapts to fit in with others, and a host who houses guests is putting them up.

clue.text: Take risks in catastrophic tennis match?

definitions.meaning: a tennis game played on a court that ends in ruin

explanation.definitionFit: To court disaster is to invite trouble by acting rashly; read literally, a disaster on the court is a tennis match gone badly wrong.

clue.text: Accident to pupil in part of church

parts.note: a chance is an accident or fluke
L, for learner, stands for a pupil, as on a learner driver's plate

explanation.surface: A mishap befalling a schoolchild inside a church.
explanation.walkthrough: L is for learner, from the L-plates British learner drivers display.
explanation.definitionFit: The chancel is the area around the altar, reserved for clergy and choir, a section of a church building.

clue.text: Tooler working around front of marksman's quiver

indicators.note: around means the reworked letters go round the next piece
working signals the letters of tooler set in motion and rearranged
front of picks the opening letter of marksman's

explanation.surface: A craftsman at work circling the place where a sniper keeps arrows.
explanation.walkthrough: 'quiver' looks like an arrow case near 'marksman', but it is the verb sense: a trembling. 'working' turns TOOLER into TREOLO, and 'around' wraps it round M, the 'front of marksman's'.
explanation.definitionFit: A tremolo is a trembling, wavering effect in music or the voice, a kind of shake.

clue.text: Reluctant to ignore low instance of bad language

indicators.note: to ignore something is to leave it out, so a letter is removed

parts.note: loath means unwilling or reluctant

explanation.surface: Someone unwilling to overlook a coarse example of swearing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to ignore' drops L (low) from LOATH.
explanation.definitionFit: An oath can mean a swear word or curse, a single piece of profanity.

clue.text: Fidelio, peradventure, providing an example?

indicators.note: providing means the words supply the letters from within them, running across the comma

explanation.surface: Fidelio, perhaps, offered as a specimen of its kind.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer runs across 'FidelIO, PERAdventure'; the whole clue also defines it, since Beethoven's Fidelio is an example. 'Peradventure' is an old word for perhaps.
explanation.definitionFit: Fidelio is Beethoven's only staged musical drama, so it is one instance of this form.

clue.text: Party men finding way to get in

parts.note: a do is a party or celebration
OR, other ranks, are soldiers who are not officers, ordinary men

explanation.surface: Partygoers looking for the entrance.
explanation.definitionFit: A door is the usual means of entry into a room or building.

clue.text: Month in which bishop is to take a partner

indicators.note: in which means the next piece goes inside the month

parts.note: May is a month
RR, Right Reverend, is the title of a bishop

explanation.surface: Naming the month when a bishop will wed.
explanation.walkthrough: RR is Right Reverend, the formal style of an Anglican bishop.
explanation.definitionFit: To marry is to wed, taking a spouse.

clue.text: Old article about people getting upset, in Time?

indicators.note: upset in a down clue means turned upside down, so the whole is read bottom to top
about means the old article goes round the next piece

parts.note: ye is an old spelling of the, the definite article
men are people

explanation.surface: An ancient piece written about people being distressed, in a magazine.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'getting upset' turns the whole build over. Time is called the old enemy in the saying, hence the question mark.
explanation.definitionFit: Time is often called the great adversary, the foe that wears all things down.

clue.text: Soldier has to show evidence of age to get commission

parts.note: a man is an ordinary soldier
a date, such as on a coin or document, shows how old something is

explanation.surface: A soldier proving how old he is before being made an officer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'commission' suggests an officer's rank, but it is the authority given to act.
explanation.definitionFit: A mandate is an official instruction or authority to act, like a commission.

clue.text: Troubled Dome accepting foreign money, perversely -that's rich

indicators.note: accepting means taking in the next piece
troubled signals the letters of dome stirred into a new order
perversely means turned the wrong way round, so the currency is read backwards

parts.note: the yen is the currency of Japan

explanation.surface: The troubled Millennium Dome taking overseas cash in a wrong-headed way.
explanation.walkthrough: The Dome is London's Millennium Dome, a troubled project; 'Troubled' rearranges it, 'perversely' turns the currency round, and 'accepting' takes it inside.
explanation.definitionFit: Moneyed means having plenty of cash, wealthy.

clue.text: Badly worded phrase originally indicated a form of precipitation

indicators.note: badly signals the letters of worded put into a disordered arrangement
originally picks the opening letter of phrase

explanation.surface: A clumsily written expression first pointed to a type of rainfall.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Badly' makes DEWDRO of WORDED, and 'originally' adds P from 'phrase'.
explanation.definitionFit: Dew condenses out of the air as moisture, and a single bead of it is a small drop of precipitation.

clue.text: Player catching end of finger in mangle

indicators.note: catching means holding the next piece inside

parts.note: a winger is a player on the wing in football or rugby

indicators.note: end of picks the last letter of finger

explanation.surface: A footballer getting a fingertip trapped in a laundry device.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mangle' looks like a verb, to crush, but it is the noun: the old roller machine for squeezing water from laundry.
explanation.definitionFit: A mangle is a machine with rollers that presses water out of washing, the same device as a wringer.

clue.text: Exophthalmous journalist meeting pontiff before end of May

indicators.note: before puts the pontiff ahead of what follows

parts.note: the pontiff is the Pope

indicators.note: end of picks the last letter of May

parts.note: ED, short for editor, is a common crossword journalist

explanation.surface: A reporter has an audience with the Pope in late May.
explanation.walkthrough: The order is POPE, then Y ('end of May'), then ED, the journalist 'meeting' them.
explanation.definitionFit: Exophthalmos is a medical condition of bulging eyeballs, so its adjective means having protruding eyes.

clue.text: Gradual spread shown by very large plant one introduced

parts.note: OS, outsize, is the clothing abbreviation for very large

indicators.note: introduced means put into the plant

parts.note: moss is a small plant
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A huge plant with a newcomer put in it, showing a slow spread.
explanation.walkthrough: OS is outsize, a clothing size label.
explanation.definitionFit: Osmosis is the slow passage of liquid through a membrane, and figuratively the gradual absorption of ideas.

clue.text: Best work — book about Greek character

parts.note: OP, opus, is the abbreviation for a musical work

indicators.note: about means the book goes round the next piece

parts.note: Tim, Timothy, is a book of the New Testament
mu is a letter of the Greek alphabet

explanation.surface: The finest piece of work is a volume on a figure from Greece.
explanation.walkthrough: 'book' is TIM, short for Timothy, one of the New Testament epistles.
explanation.definitionFit: Optimum means most favourable or ideal, the top choice.

clue.text: Zealous aunt's off to church

indicators.note: off means the letters of aunt's go wrong and are rearranged

parts.note: the possessive here supplies its S as a letter

explanation.surface: A devout aunt is heading off to a service.
explanation.walkthrough: 'off' looks like 'leaving for' in the surface but signals the rearranging; the possessive's S is needed as a letter here.
explanation.definitionFit: A staunch supporter is loyal and committed, a fervent one.

clue.text: Money found outside hospital? That's unconvincing

indicators.note: found outside means the money goes round the next piece

parts.note: tin is old British slang for money
H is the abbreviation for hospital, as on road signs

explanation.surface: Cash discovered outside a hospital, a doubtful story.
explanation.walkthrough: TIN is dated British slang for cash.
explanation.definitionFit: A thin excuse is weak and unpersuasive, hard to believe.

clue.text: Bad feeling emerging from coal-mine in Kent?

indicators.note: in means the mine sits inside the county

parts.note: Kent is a county in South East England, so it gives SE
a pit is a coal mine

explanation.surface: Ill will arising from a colliery in a southern English county.
explanation.walkthrough: Kent is a county in the South East of England, abbreviated SE; it had coal mines until the 1980s.
explanation.definitionFit: Spite is malice, a desire to hurt others.

clue.text: Platform finally rejected composite

annotationWithheld.why: Clue held as 'Platform finally rejected composite (4)': 'finally rejected' gives D, but no reading of 'composite' gives AIS or any piece to complete DAIS; likely an OCR or print error, and no other print was found.

clue.text: Graduate holding books raised subject of particle physics

indicators.note: raised in a down clue means read upwards, so backwards
holding means the graduate contains the next piece

parts.note: MA, Master of Arts, is a graduate
OT, Old Testament, is a set of books

explanation.surface: A graduate with an armful of books looking up a topic in physics.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'raised' reads the whole build from the bottom up.
explanation.definitionFit: Particle physics studies the tiny components of matter, starting from the smallest unit of an element.

clue.text: Ecdysiast's rear featured in tabloid-shock!

indicators.note: featured in means the letter appears inside the newspaper

parts.note: the Sun is a British tabloid newspaper

indicators.note: rear picks the last letter of Ecdysiast's, before the possessive

explanation.surface: A stripper's bottom appears in a tabloid, to everyone's outrage.
explanation.walkthrough: An ecdysiast is a stripper (from the Greek for shedding skin); 'rear' gives the T of 'Ecdysiast'. The Sun is a British tabloid paper.
explanation.definitionFit: To stun is to daze or astonish, to shock.

clue.text: Austen character read aloud every evening

indicators.note: read aloud means the name is spoken, giving a word that sounds the same

parts.note: Mr Knightley is the hero of Jane Austen's Emma

explanation.surface: Someone reciting a Jane Austen hero's lines each night.
explanation.walkthrough: The K of Knightley is silent, so the name sounds like the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Nightly means happening each night, occurring every evening.

clue.text: Tenor in US state finally gave performance

indicators.note: in means the tenor goes inside the state

parts.note: Maine is a US state
T is the abbreviation for tenor in vocal scores

indicators.note: finally picks the last letter of gave

explanation.surface: A tenor in New England at last put on a show.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' puts T inside MAINE; 'finally' adds the E of 'gave'.
explanation.definitionFit: A matinee is an afternoon showing of a play or film, a performance.

clue.text: Bond swallowing medicinal draught endlessly-a man's drink

indicators.note: swallowing means the bond takes the next piece inside

parts.note: cement is a bond, something that binds

indicators.note: endlessly removes the last letter of the remedy

parts.note: a remedy is a medicine one drinks
he is the pronoun for a man

explanation.surface: James Bond downing a cure-all, a liqueur for men.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bond' suggests James Bond, agent 007, but is the binding sense; 'endlessly' drops the cure's last letter before 'swallowing' takes it in.
explanation.definitionFit: Crème de menthe is a sweet mint-flavoured liqueur, an alcoholic beverage.
